content.text:
While the random search runs, let me think about a more principled design to try in parallel via reasoning.

The structure is a multiloop with 9 branches off the outer 15-bp stem, then 5 sub-branches each. The cross-arm pairing problem: adjacent arms in a multiloop share their 3'/5' ends. If arm A's 5'strand (read 5'->3') equals the reverse complement of arm B's 3'strand... Actually for two arms A and B both opening to the right of a junction, spurious pairing A_5strand with B_3strand occurs when A_5strand is complementary (anti-parallel) to B_3strand. Since B_3strand = reverse(complement(B_5strand)), A_5strand complementary to B_3strand means A_5strand = reverse(B_5strand). 

Hmm, that's the condition. So to avoid: ensure no two arms have 5'strands that are reverses of each other. With 2-bp words, w and reverse(w) — pairs like GG/GG(same), GC/CG, GA/AG, GU/UG, CC/CC, CA/AC, CU/UC, AA/AA, AU/UA, UU/UU. So distinct reverses needed. There are many 2-nt words; picking one from each reverse-pair gives ~8 options but we have 20 two-bp stems. So collisions unavoidable among the 5 sub-arms within a single branch — but they're separated by junctions so may not actually interact.

Actually the cross-pairing seen in the naive result was between arms in DIFFERENT branches (16-372 etc.), i.e. arms far apart pairing across the whole molecule. That's because all stems were G...C, making every 5'strand = G's and every 3'strand = C's, so all 5'strands pair with all 3'strands.

The fix: make stems varied. The random search tests this. Let me also prepare a deterministic "good" candidate: use a rotating set of stem words so adjacent arms differ. Let me wait for monitor output first.
